items.followUp: State two reasons why organisms are classified.

rubric.why: Classification groups organisms by their shared and differing characteristics.
rubric.description: States that classification groups organisms according to similarities and differences.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that organisms are grouped by their similarities and/or differences.

rubric.why: Classification makes the identification and study of organisms easier and helps show their relationships.
rubric.description: Gives a purpose of classification, such as easier identification or study, or showing relationships.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid purpose.

modelAnswer: Classification groups organisms according to their similarities and differences.
It makes organisms easier to identify and study, and helps show relationships among them.

items.followUp: Explain how scientific names help scientists communicate about organisms.

rubric.why: A species has one accepted scientific name used internationally.
rubric.description: States that binomial nomenclature gives organisms a universal or internationally accepted name.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the universal nature of scientific names.

rubric.why: Using one scientific name avoids confusion caused by different local or common names.
rubric.description: Explains that scientific names avoid confusion and support clear communication.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining how this improves communication.

modelAnswer: Binomial nomenclature gives each species one universal scientific name used internationally.
It avoids confusion caused by different common or local names, making scientific communication clear.

items.followUp: What does it mean if a species is extinct? Give one example.

rubric.why: An endangered species has a very small or declining population and faces a risk of extinction.
rubric.description: Defines an endangered species as one threatened with extinction or at serious risk because its population is declining.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition.

rubric.why: The answer must name two endangered species found in Pakistan.
rubric.description: Gives two examples of endangered species of Pakistan.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for two valid examples.

modelAnswer: A species is called endangered when its population has declined so much that it faces a risk of extinction.
Examples of endangered species in Pakistan include the Indus river dolphin and the snow leopard.

items.followUp: What happens to homologous chromosomes during crossing over?

rubric.why: Crossing over involves the exchange of chromosome segments between homologous chromosomes.
rubric.description: States that homologous chromosomes exchange corresponding segments during crossing over.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the exchange between homologous chromosomes.

rubric.why: The exchange produces new combinations of alleles, increasing variation among offspring.
rubric.description: Links crossing over to new allele combinations or genetic diversity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the effect on genetic diversity.

modelAnswer: During meiosis, homologous chromosomes exchange corresponding segments.
This creates new combinations of alleles and increases genetic diversity in the offspring.

items.followUp: What role does mitosis play in the growth and repair of an organism?

rubric.why: Mitosis produces new cells for replacement.
rubric.description: Identifies mitosis or cell division as the process that produces replacement cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming the process.

rubric.why: New cells replace cells that are worn out, damaged, or dead.
rubric.description: States that replacement cells take the place of worn-out, damaged, or dead cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the purpose of replacement.

modelAnswer: Cell replacement occurs by mitosis, which produces new cells.
The new cells replace worn-out, damaged, or dead cells.

items.followUp: What is the end product of glycolysis, and where in the cell does it occur?

rubric.why: Glycolysis is the breakdown of glucose to form pyruvic acid.
rubric.description: Defines glycolysis as the breakdown of glucose into pyruvic acid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the process and its product.

rubric.why: Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm of the cell.
rubric.description: Gives the cellular location of glycolysis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct location.

modelAnswer: Glycolysis is the breakdown of glucose into pyruvic acid.
It takes place in the cytoplasm of the cell.

items.followUp: Describe how the rate of photosynthesis changes as light intensity increases.

rubric.why: As temperature rises, photosynthesis speeds up until the optimum temperature is reached.
rubric.description: States that the rate increases as temperature rises up to an optimum.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the increase up to the optimum.

rubric.why: Above the optimum, the rate falls because high temperatures affect or denature the enzymes involved.
rubric.description: States that the rate decreases above the optimum, preferably explaining the effect on enzymes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the decrease above the optimum or its enzyme-based reason.

modelAnswer: As temperature rises, the rate of photosynthesis increases up to an optimum temperature.
Above the optimum, the rate decreases because high temperatures affect the enzymes involved in photosynthesis.

items.followUp: How does the induced fit model explain the binding of a substrate to an enzyme?

rubric.why: In the lock and key model, the enzyme's active site has a fixed shape complementary to the substrate.
rubric.description: Describes the lock and key model as a fixed active site that fits the substrate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the fixed, complementary fit.

rubric.why: In the induced fit model, substrate binding causes the flexible active site to change shape and fit the substrate.
rubric.description: Describes the induced fit model as involving a flexible active site that changes shape on binding.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the change in active-site shape.

modelAnswer: In the lock and key model, the enzyme's active site has a fixed shape that fits the substrate exactly.
In the induced fit model, the active site is flexible and changes shape to fit the substrate when it binds.
